tip.title: Is the reasoning sound?
tip.text: Evaluating an argument means more than finding the claim. Ask: (1) Is the evidence relevant to THIS claim? (2) Is it sufficient, or just one example? (3) Is the source credible? (4) Does the reasoning actually connect evidence to claim, or does it jump? Watch for common faults: overgeneralizing from a few cases, assuming that because B came after A, A caused B, appealing to emotion instead of facts, and attacking the person rather than the idea.

passage.title: Ban Phones in Class? Two Letters
passage.text:
LETTER ONE
Phones must be banned from every classroom in our school. Last month a student in Grade 9 was caught watching videos during a quiz. Clearly, phones destroy learning. Any teacher who disagrees simply does not care about discipline. Our grandparents learned without phones and turned out fine. If we do not act now, our school's reputation will be ruined forever.

LETTER TWO
I understand the worry about phones, but a total ban would be a mistake. A 2021 study of 1,200 students in Metro Manila found that classes which used phones for structured tasks, such as timed quizzes and vocabulary apps, scored slightly higher on end-of-term tests than classes with no phone use, while classes with unrestricted phone use scored lowest. The problem, then, is not the device but the rules around it. I propose a "phones face-down unless the teacher says otherwise" policy, with confiscation for repeat violations. This keeps the benefits, removes most distractions, and teaches students the self-control they will need in any workplace. We should also track results for one semester and revisit the policy if scores drop.

words.meaning: what people generally think about someone or something
words.example: The school has a reputation for good science teaching.
The pass gives unrestricted access to the library.

words.meaning: taking something away as a penalty
words.example: Confiscation of the toy ended the fight.

items.prompt: What is the main weakness of Letter One's evidence?
choices: It uses too many statistics.
It generalizes from a single student's behavior to all phones and all students.
It is too long.
It quotes a study that is too old.
items.why: One Grade 9 student watching videos is used to conclude "phones destroy learning" for everyone. That is overgeneralization.

items.prompt: "Any teacher who disagrees simply does not care about discipline." What fault is this?
choices: Attacking the people who disagree instead of their reasons
Giving too much evidence
Using a study
Proposing a trial period
items.why: It dismisses opponents by questioning their character rather than answering their argument.

items.prompt: Why is Letter Two's study stronger evidence than Letter One's example?
choices: It is about Manila.
It covers 1,200 students, compares different conditions, and measures results.
It is more recent than last month.
It uses bigger words.
items.why: Size, comparison groups, and measured outcomes make evidence more reliable than one anecdote.

items.prompt: Why does the writer of Letter One include the sentence "If we do not act now, our school's reputation will be ruined forever"?
choices: To report a measured result from last month
To define what reputation means
To propose a fair test of the policy
To frighten readers into agreeing before they ask for proof
items.why: The sentence predicts disaster with no support; its job is to create fear, not to give evidence.

items.prompt: Which feature makes Letter Two's reasoning more careful?
choices: It says phones are perfect.
It suggests tracking results for a semester and revisiting the policy.
It mentions grandparents.
It bans phones completely.
items.why: Planning to check results and change course shows the writer is testing the claim, not just asserting it.

items.prompt: What do the two letters have in COMMON?
choices: Both want a complete ban.
Both agree that unrestricted phone use in class is a problem.
Both cite a study.
Both attack teachers.
items.why: Letter One wants a ban; Letter Two also says unrestricted use scores lowest and proposes rules to limit it.

items.prompt: How do the two letters DIFFER in the solution they propose?
choices: Letter One wants phones used for quizzes; Letter Two wants them banned.
Both want a trial period, but for different lengths.
Letter One wants a total ban; Letter Two wants rules that allow structured use.
Letter One wants confiscation; Letter Two wants no penalties at all.
items.why: Letter One says phones "must be banned from every classroom"; Letter Two proposes "phones face-down unless the teacher says otherwise."

items.prompt: How do the two writers differ in the way they treat people who disagree with them?
choices: Both ignore the other side completely.
Letter One says they "do not care about discipline"; Letter Two begins by saying "I understand the worry."
Letter One quotes them; Letter Two insults them.
Letter One thanks them; Letter Two threatens them.
items.why: Letter One dismisses teachers who disagree; Letter Two opens by acknowledging the other side's concern before arguing against a ban.

items.prompt: Why does the writer of Letter Two include the 2021 study of 1,200 students?
choices: To show that the problem is the rules around phones, not the device itself
To prove that Metro Manila schools are better
To entertain readers with an interesting fact
To argue that all phone use should be unrestricted
items.why: Right after the study, the writer says, "The problem, then, is not the device but the rules around it." The study is there to support that point.

items.prompt: What is the MAIN purpose that BOTH letters share?
choices: To inform readers about how a 2021 study was done
To persuade the school to adopt the writer's phone policy
To entertain readers with stories about students
To explain how to use vocabulary apps in class
items.why: Letter One says phones "must be banned"; Letter Two says "I propose" a face-down policy. Each writer wants the school to act on their plan.
